Ambient gRNA assignment: a comparative review of geomux, fishash, and CLEANSER

Models, datasets, what each gets right and wrong — with a re-analysis of CLEANSER on our SCEPTRE3 simulations

Author

gRNA-assignment investigation (sceptre3)

Published

June 26, 2026

Executive summary

This report consolidates a close reading of the three leading “ambient-aware” guide-assignment methods — geomux, fishash, and CLEANSER — against the datasets they analyzed, their conclusions, and our own cross-dataset measurements, and ends with a re-analysis of why CLEANSER appeared to fail on our SCEPTRE3 simulations.

Bottom line / recommendation. Grounded in real barnyard ground truth and FDR experiments across Simpson \(\times\) overdispersion \(\times\) MOI regimes: adopt fishash’s contingency core (Fisher test + Simpson correction + Guo–Sarkar FDR), plus one canonical improvement of our own — decontaminate the cell margin (use ambient depth, not library size). fishash decontaminates the guide margin but uses the raw, signal-contaminated library size as each cell’s ambient exposure; our cross-dataset work shows that’s wrong, and the symmetric fix beats fishash at MOI ≥ 1 (it recovers the recall fishash loses) while tying at low MOI and on real barnyard, at controlled FDR. It targets fishash’s documented high-MOI weak spot. Two from-scratch alternatives were tested and rejected: a marginal NB method (it is dominated — conditioning beats marginal), and an overdispersion tail (works on sims but its φ is not robustly estimable on real data — keep fishash’s hypergeometric). The simple ambient test stays as a fast high-signal default, but it is not FDR-calibrated and is not the flagship.

Five supporting takeaways:

  1. All three are the same idea with different machinery. Each assigns guide g to cell c when its UMI count exceeds an ambient null whose mean factorizes as \(\lambda_{g,c} = \gamma_g \cdot \kappa_c\) — a guide ambient share \(\gamma_g\) times a cell ambient depth \(\kappa_c\). geomux and fishash test against this null with a Fisher/hypergeometric test (contingency-table view); CLEANSER fits it as a per-guide Bayesian negative-binomial mixture. Our ambient-proportion test is the shared statistical core.

  2. fishash is the current state of the art on real ground truth — the only method strong on both CROP-seq and direct-capture barnyard data — because it adds two corrections to the plain test: a Simpson’s-paradox correction (cell/guide-margin contamination) and a block-dependent FDR correction. We reproduced its Simpson phenomenon exactly.

  3. geomux = our ambient test + a heuristic log-odds threshold. It is fast and well-calibrated at low MOI but its published benchmark is thin (simulation-only, one competitor) and it collapses on direct-capture data (it stops assigning).

  4. CLEANSER’s distinctive contributions are empirical and on-target for us: it is built on an experimentally-validated ambient characterization, it normalizes per-cell depth with exactly our \(\kappa_c\) (the sub-threshold UMI sum), and it models overdispersion (NB ambient for direct-capture). Its costs are MCMC runtime, per-guide independence (no cross-guide sharing of the ambient pool), and heavy prior dependence.

  5. CLEANSER did not underperform on our SCEPTRE3 sims — the benchmark mis-scored it. The scoring function counted every guide–cell pair CLEANSER emitted a posterior for as a positive assignment, never applying the posterior threshold. Re-scoring the same output files at the standard 0.5 cutoff turns its reported Jaccard of 0.43 → 0.89 (precision 0.99). This is a one-line fix in our analysis code, not a flaw in CLEANSER.

1 The unifying framework

Treat the gRNA count matrix as \(N_{g,c}\) = UMIs of guide \(g\) in cell \(c\), with margins \(N_{g,\cdot}\) (guide total), \(N_{\cdot,c}\) (cell total / library size), \(N\) (grand total). Assignment asks, for each pair, whether \(N_{g,c}\) is larger than ambient contamination alone would produce.

The ambient (noise) process is, to first order, a rank-1 Poisson field:

\[\mathbb{E}\big[N^{\text{noise}}_{g,c}\big] \;=\; \gamma_g \cdot \kappa_c, \qquad \textstyle\sum_g \gamma_g = 1,\]

where \(\gamma_g\) is guide \(g\)’s share of the ambient pool (a single composition vector) and \(\kappa_c\) is cell \(c\)’s ambient capture depth. Everything below is a different way to (a) estimate this rank-1 field and (b) test a count against it.

how it estimates \(\gamma_g\) how it estimates \(\kappa_c\) the test extra machinery
simple per-guide threshold (Otsu, valley) — (ignores guides jointly) — (ignores cell depth) per-guide bimodal cut on log counts none
ambient test (ours) global share \(N_{g,\cdot}/N\) library size \(N_{\cdot,c}\) one-sided Poisson/hypergeometric, BH one knob (FDR \(q\))
geomux guide margin \(N_{g,\cdot}\) cell margin \(N_{\cdot,c}\) one-sided hypergeometric, BH adaptive log-odds-ratio per-cell gate
fishash noise-only profile (rank-1 Poisson completion) column margin \(N_{\cdot,c}\) hypergeometric on the noise-conditioned table Simpson correction + Guo–Sarkar block FDR
CLEANSER per-guide fitted rate \(\lambda_j\) / \(\mu_{j,\text{noise}}\) \(L_i\) = sub-threshold UMI sum per-guide NB mixture, MCMC posterior overdispersion (\(\phi\)), Bayesian priors

The spectrum runs simple test → contingency table (geomux, fishash) → mixture model (CLEANSER). geomux and fishash sit at the same node; fishash is strictly more sophisticated (geomux adds only a threshold; fishash adds two principled corrections). CLEANSER is the generative pole — it models both the noise and the signal distribution per guide, buying overdispersion-robustness at the price of MCMC and per-guide independence.

2 The three methods in depth

2.1 geomux — contingency test + a log-odds gate

Source. Teyssier (2024), UCSF PhD dissertation, Ch. 5; code noamteyssier/geomux (v0.5.5); simulator muxsim. The geomux method chapter is simulation-only.

Model. On a cell×guide matrix, after QC (\(\geq 5\) UMI per cell/guide), each count is tested under a hypergeometric null parameterized by the table margins, \(N_{g,c}\sim\text{Hypergeometric}(N,\,N_{\cdot,c},\,N_{g,\cdot})\) — i.e. exactly the rank-1 ambient null with \(\gamma_g = N_{g,\cdot}/N\), \(\kappa_c = N_{\cdot,c}\). P-values are BH-adjusted. The only addition beyond the ambient test is a per-cell log-odds-ratio gate: guides are sorted by adjusted p-value and iteratively demoted to “noise” if their logit gap to the most-significant insignificant guide falls below a threshold \(T_L\) (fixed \(=1\) in the dissertation; adaptive in current code, an undocumented adaptive_lor_scalar). No block FDR, no overdispersion, no doublet model.

Datasets. None real in the method chapter — 3,456 parameter combinations of muxsim multinomial simulations with an equiprobable ambient background (unrealistic). Real applications appear only in other chapters (dementia CROP-seq screen, GSE207099; an ASD CROP-seq screen, accession not stated).

Benchmark. A single competitor — demuxEM (a cell-hashing demultiplexer, not a guide-assignment SOTA) — on MOI-level metrics (accuracy = fraction of cells with correctly predicted MOI). geomux beats demuxEM at MOI \(\leq 2\) and is ~10× faster; demuxEM wins at MOI \(> 2\) (author-stated).

Right. Statistically motivated, interpretable, few knobs; conditions on both margins (the two first-order ambient effects); excellent FDR control and speed; the log-odds gate is a sensible per-cell signal-to-noise filter.

Wrong / limits. Benchmark is thin (one non-comparable competitor, simulation-only, MOI-level metrics, no per-guide precision/recall, no comparison to crispat/CLEANSER/sceptre/fishash). The equiprobable-background simulator flatters it. The pooled signal+noise null makes it the uncorrected Simpson curve (see §[Simpson]). On real barnyard data it collapses on direct-capture (it assigns nothing in many cells — accuracy 0.75/0.53; fishash Table 2). The threshold is not principled in the paper.

2.2 fishash — the corrected contingency method (current SOTA)

Source. Kamm, Yeung & Forrest (2026), bioRxiv 2026.01.22.701179; package jackkamm/fishash (v0.99.0). Defaults: padj_method="GS", refit=10.

Model. A one-sided Fisher/hypergeometric test per \((g,c)\), plus two corrections:

  • Simpson’s-paradox correction. The plain test pools signal and noise; for a low-signal guide this can flip the \(2\times2\) odds ratio above 1 even when the guide is truly absent (Prop. 1, Fig. 2). fishash replaces the “other-cells” counts with noise-only counts (adjusted odds ratio \(R^*\), Eq. 7), estimating the latent noise counts by rank-1 Poisson matrix completion of the assigned-masked matrix (Eq. 9), iterated with a mask schedule (Alg. 1). This is a direct, transparent estimate of the rank-1 ambient field \(\gamma_g\kappa_c\) from the noise.
  • Guo–Sarkar (2020) block FDR. Because hypergeometric components within a cell are negatively associated (violating BH’s PRDS), fishash uses a per-cell block correction, not plain BH.

fishash(refit=0) = the plain Fisher test = geomux’s core = our ambient test.

Datasets. (i) Barnyard (Liu 2025, GSE272457) — species-mixing CROP-seq + direct-capture, the canonical real ground truth (Table 2). (ii) Replogle 2022 genome-wide K562 (figshare 20127869), with a proxy truth (paired dual-guide co-occurrence). (iii) A CellBender-based simulator (guidebender) sweeping #guides (Fig. 5), MOI (Fig. 6), and signal–noise correlation (Fig. 7, Simpson). The bundled Schraivogel object is only a package test fixture, not used in the figures.

Benchmark (the most complete in the field). Comparators: CLEANSER, crispat (4 mixtures), DemuxEM, geomux 0.5.5, SCEPTRE. Headline numbers:

  • Barnyard Table 2 (CROP-0hr / CROP-72hr / DC-0hr / DC-72hr): fishash 0.956 / 0.953 / 0.910 / 0.949 — only method strong on all four. geomux wins CROP-seq narrowly (0.958 / 0.956) but collapses on DC (0.747 / 0.525). crispat-PoissonGauss ~0.95 (CROP only).
  • Replogle proxy: fishash highest F1 in 78% of 273 runs, highest recall (median 97%); but no method exceeds ~71% precision (proxy-truth ceiling from promoter silencing).
  • Sims (Fig. 5): fishash controls FDR (precision \(\geq 0.95\)) in all 100 simulations; geomux fails nominal FDR, especially in the low-expression regime.
  • Sims (Fig. 6, MOI): fishash best for MOI \(\leq 0.5\); dcCLEANSER best for \(1 \leq\) MOI \(\leq 3\); crispat-PoissonGauss best for MOI \(\geq 5\). No method dominates everywhere.
  • Resources (Fig. 8): fishash & geomux are the cheapest (seconds, <1 GiB) even at 80,000 guides.

Right. Best real-data accuracy across chemistries; reproducible FDR control; the Simpson correction removes false positives without costing recall (we reproduced this — §[Simpson]); excellent scalability; unusually honest reporting (publishes where competitors win).

Wrong / limits (mostly stated). The hypergeometric core assumes conditional equidispersion; under overdispersed noise the authors’ own Appendix C shows fishash loses FDR control — and direct-capture ambient is overdispersed (CLEANSER’s finding). The method is iterative with a hand-tuned mask schedule; the noise model is rank-1 while their generative model is rank-2 (an acknowledged estimator/model mismatch); and there is no fully-known-truth real dataset (barnyard is high-signal cell lines; Replogle truth is a proxy).

2.3 CLEANSER — the validated mixture model

Source. Liu, Hamilton et al. (2025), Cell Genomics 5:100766; repo Gersbachlab-Bioinformatics/CLEANSER.

Empirical foundation (its real contribution). A human/mouse dCas9-KRAB barnyard screen (MOI ~10) with species-specific non-targeting libraries gives provable ambient labels (a guide in the wrong species is ambient). Findings: ambient is droplet/prep-borne, not co-culture exchange; ambient UMIs correlate with native UMIs; transduced-vs-ambient separation is 7–13× for CROP-seq but 50–266× for direct-capture; and — the modeling crux — CROP-seq ambient is ~Poisson but direct-capture ambient is overdispersed (NB).

Model. A per-guide, zero-truncated two-component mixture fit by Stan MCMC:

  • csCLEANSER (CROP-seq): \(X_i \sim (1-r)\,\text{Poisson}(\lambda) + r\,\text{NB}(\mu,\phi)\).
  • dcCLEANSER (direct-capture): \(X_i \sim (1-r)\,\text{NB}(\mu_0,\phi_0) + r\,\text{NB}(\mu_1,\phi_1)\).

with a hard constraint \(\mu_{\text{signal}} > \lambda_{\text{noise}}\), a strong \(r\sim\text{Beta}(1,10)\) prior (most pairs are ambient), and a cell normalization \(L_i\) = the cell’s sum of gRNA UMIs \(\leq 2\), normalized to mean 1; means scale as \(\lambda_{ij} = \lambda_j L_i\), \(\mu_{ij} = \mu_j L_i\). Output is the posterior \(P(\text{native} \mid X_i)\) per pair; assignment thresholds it (defaults 0.8 CROP-seq, 0.5 direct-capture).

This is our framework, generatively. \(L_i\) is our cell depth \(\kappa_c\) (the sub-threshold UMI sum); \(\lambda_j\) / \(\mu_{j,\text{noise}}\) plays the role of \(\gamma_g\) (the guide ambient rate) — but fitted independently per guide, losing the rank-1 cross-guide tie. csCLEANSER’s Poisson ambient \(\lambda_j L_i\) is exactly our ambient mean \(\gamma_g\kappa_c\); dcCLEANSER generalizes it to NB — the one thing a rank-1 Poisson null cannot do.

Datasets. Its own barnyard (GSE272457, have it); reprocessed Gasperini 2019 (GSE120861, BAM-only); McCutcheon 2023 CD8 T-cell direct-capture (GSE218988); Chardon 2023 K562 CRISPRa direct-capture (processed matrices on washington.edu).

Benchmark. Versus a strict UMI cutoff and the 10X Mixture Model only (no SCEPTRE/geomux/fishash). Validation is indirect — downstream DE hits + small-n RT-qPCR, and “% non-transduced retained” on the barnyard — rather than a precision/recall table. Claims 32 extra CRISPRa hits vs the 10X model, 4/6 unique hits qPCR-validated.

Right. Empirically-grounded depth normalization (\(L_i\!=\!\kappa_c\), validated against ambient load); data-driven overdispersion (Poisson vs NB by platform); the only method trained on known ambient; open and editable; soft-probability output.

Wrong / limits. MCMC cost (per-guide Stan; zero-truncation was needed just for tractability — poor fit for genome scale); per-guide independence (no shared ambient pool, the central contrast with the contingency view); no Simpson/contingency correction; heavy prior dependence tuned to HEK293T/NIH3T3 at MOI 10 (on the low-UMI T-cell data the posterior cutoff had to be hand-dropped to 0.08); a fixed \(\leq 2\) normalization threshold; weak validation (no head-to-head accuracy table on the ground truth it generated).

3 Head-to-head: what each gets right and wrong

dimension geomux fishash CLEANSER
statistical core hypergeometric test hypergeometric test NB mixture (MCMC)
per-cell depth \(\kappa_c\) column margin (implicit) column margin (implicit) explicit \(L_i\) = sub-threshold sum
per-guide ambient \(\gamma_g\) row margin (pooled) noise-only, rank-1 completion per-guide fit (no sharing)
Simpson/contamination ✗ (uncorrected) ✔ correction ✗
overdispersion ✗ ✗ (equidispersed; fails in App. C) ✔ NB ambient
multiple testing BH Guo–Sarkar block Bayesian posterior
real ground-truth accuracy CROP-seq good, DC collapses best on both chemistries not tabulated vs truth
speed / scale excellent excellent poor (MCMC)
principal weakness thin benchmark, no DC, uncorrected overdispersion (App. C) cost, priors, per-guide

The cleanest synthesis: fishash and CLEANSER address orthogonal failure modes of the plain test. fishash fixes the mean (Simpson contamination of the rank-1 field) but keeps an equidispersed tail; CLEANSER fixes the variance (NB overdispersion) but keeps a contaminated, per-guide mean and no contingency correction. Neither fixes both. geomux fixes neither (it is the plain test plus a threshold). A method that estimated a decontaminated rank-1 ambient field and used an overdispersion-robust (or nonparametric) tail would dominate both — this is the design target.

4 Our cross-dataset empirical findings

We measured the two halves of the ambient field — depth \(\kappa_c\) and composition \(\gamma_g\) — across 17 real datasets (10 perturb-seq survey datasets, Gasperini, Replogle, Schraivogel, 4 barnyard samples). The picture both supports and sharpens the methods above.

Depth is not library size — universally. A cell’s gRNA library is ~89–100% its own real integration, so naive library size overstates ambient depth by a median 51× (range 2.7–424×) and is nearly uncorrelated with it at low MOI (Panel A–B). This is exactly why CLEANSER’s \(L_i\) and fishash’s column-margin normalization matter, and why a plain count threshold fails. CLEANSER’s sub-threshold estimator recovers the true ambient depth well (median \(r=0.81\)) except on very deep direct-capture (its fixed \(\leq 2\) threshold misses ambient when counts routinely exceed 2 — Panel D), arguing for a depth-adaptive threshold.

Composition is uneven, and its contamination scales with library complexity. The ambient pool spans ~10–40× across guides (Gini median 0.43; Panel C). The naive global share is an unbiased proxy for the true ambient share on average, but its variance grows with library size — in an 86-guide screen 100% of guides agree within 2×, in a 6800-guide iPSC library only 63% do. This is the guide-margin Simpson contamination fishash corrects and geomux/CLEANSER do not.

We reproduced fishash’s Simpson phenomenon (Fig. 7) using its own simulator and package: the uncorrected test (= our ambient core) inflates FDR to ~0.20 and fails the nominal 5% in 10/10 reps when ambient composition is uncorrelated with signal; the correction restores FDR to 0.003 with unchanged recall.

5 CLEANSER on our SCEPTRE3 sims: the “underperformance” is a scoring artifact

The reported result. In our lab benchmark (assignment-writeup.Rmd), CLEANSER on the replogle-rd7_simulated sims looked dramatically worse than SCEPTRE/crispat:

sim method Jaccard precision recall
1.5% Pert (25 guides) SCEPTRE 0.93 0.96 0.97
1.5% Pert (25 guides) crispat 0.95 0.98 0.97
1.5% Pert (25 guides) CLEANSER 0.43 0.43 0.995
0.5% Pert (10 guides) CLEANSER 0.22 0.22 0.997

The signature — precision \(\approx\) Jaccard, recall \(\approx 1\) — is pure over-assignment: CLEANSER appears to call almost everything.

The diagnosis. The over-assignment is an artifact of how the benchmark read CLEANSER’s output, not of CLEANSER. The runner run_cleanser.py writes a posterior for every guide–cell pair with a nonzero count (the zero-truncated model conditions on count \(> 0\)). The scoring function then does:

process_clns <- function(clns_output_fp, assn_list, ground_truth) {
  clns_assign_raw <- read.csv(clns_output_fp)
  unordered_cell_list <- split(clns_assign_raw$cell_id, clns_assign_raw$grna_id)  # <- takes ALL cells
  ...                                                                              # <- never filters on `posterior`
}

It takes every cell_id in the file as an assignment — it never thresholds posterior. So CLEANSER’s output is collapsed to “assign if count \(\geq 1\).” (Tellingly, the commented-out process_clns_parts did threshold at posterior > 0.8; the active path dropped it.)

The proof. The arithmetic matches exactly: the output file has 83,851 recorded pairs, the sim has 36,418 true perturbations, and \(36418 / 83851 = 0.434\) = the reported “precision.” Re-scoring the same CLEANSER output file at the standard 0.5 posterior threshold:

reported (no threshold) re-scored (posterior > 0.5)
1.5% Pert precision 0.43, Jaccard 0.43 precision 0.988, recall 0.903, Jaccard 0.893

CLEANSER’s false positives at the 0.5 cutoff are a small number of genuine ambient-tail cells (median raw count 5, all \(\geq 3\)), and it correctly rejects the large majority of them. At the standard threshold CLEANSER is competitive with SCEPTRE and crispat on these sims.

The corrected benchmark. Re-scoring the same CLEANSER output files at the proper threshold (0.5 for --dc), per-guide, reproduces the writeup’s buggy numbers exactly when un-thresholded (validating the scorer) and gives the corrected result:

sim SCEPTRE crispat pertpy CLEANSER (buggy) CLEANSER (fixed)
1.5% pert, 25 guides 0.93 0.96 0.08 0.43 0.89
0.5% pert, 10 guides 0.93 0.95 0.11 0.22 0.95

(Jaccard; results/benchmark_update/cleanser_corrected.csv.) Corrected CLEANSER is competitive with SCEPTRE and crispat — it ties crispat on the 0.5%-pert sim. Its real cost is runtime (~14–50 min MCMC vs SCEPTRE’s 0.2 min). The “CLEANSER underperforms” conclusion was a one-line scoring bug, not a property of CLEANSER.

Action taken. We downloaded the most valuable genuinely-missing, feasibly-downloadable dataset: McCutcheon 2023 (GSE218988) — a direct-capture CD8 T-cell CRISPRi screen that CLEANSER used and where it was most fragile. A CRISPRi donor’s processed CellRanger output (~382 MB) was pulled and the CRISPR-Guide-Capture submatrix extracted to ~/data/external/mccutcheon-2023-GSE218988/grna_matrix.rds (40 guides × 22,100 cells, median library just 8 UMIs — confirming the very-low-UMI direct-capture regime where CLEANSER needed a hand-dropped 0.08 cutoff). This is exactly where our analysis predicts overdispersion matters most, and we held few such datasets; it is ready to fold into the cross-dataset depth/composition sweep. (geomux’s GSE207099 exposes only assignment tables, not count matrices; Gasperini/Replogle full raw sets require CellRanger reprocessing and we already hold calibrated references/sims; the Chardon CRISPRa matrices remain an easy future add.)

7 Build vs. adopt: an experimental test

The analysis above suggested an opening: a method fixing both failure modes — a decontaminated rank-1 ambient mean (fishash’s strength) and an overdispersion-robust tail (CLEANSER’s strength) — as a fast closed-form test. I implemented exactly that candidate (scripts/ambient_nb_method.R): estimate \(\gamma_g\kappa_c\) from noise-masked margins (the mean fix), then test each count against \(\text{NB}(\gamma_g\kappa_c,\phi)\) with a single overdispersion \(\phi\) estimated from the ambient residuals (\(\phi\!\to\!0\) recovers the Poisson ambient test). One knob, fast, auto-adapting Poisson\(\leftrightarrow\)NB. Then I benchmarked it head-to-head against the plain ambient test and fishash, on (i) the authors’ simulator across the Simpson \(\times\) overdispersion grid and (ii) the real barnyard ground truth.

The result is decisive — and negative for “build.”

  • The plain ambient test does not control FDR on any simulator regime (realized FDR 0.06–0.40). Its apparent wins elsewhere come from forgiving per-cell metrics on high-signal data, not rigorous per-guide FDR.
  • fishash controls FDR at recall \(\approx\) 0.95 across Simpson and overdispersion, the only method in the good corner of the trade-off. (Its lone simulator wobble — pure overdispersion, 1/5 reps — does not appear on real overdispersed data: see below.)
  • The NB candidate is dominated. A single global overdispersion parameter is caught between over-conservatism (global \(\phi\) → FDR controlled but recall ≈ 0.4) and anti-conservatism (robust \(\phi\) → recall ≈ 0.95 but FDR ≈ 0.1–0.2). No tuning of a plug-in \(\phi\) attains both; fishash’s conditional contingency test calibrates without estimating \(\phi\) at all.

Real-data confirmation (barnyard, Table-2 accuracy):

CROP 0hr CROP 72hr DC 0hr DC 72hr mean
ambient (Poisson) 0.935 0.964 0.953 0.948 0.950
fishash 0.909 0.949 0.957 0.953 0.942
NB candidate 0.489 0.544 0.000 0.101 0.284

The candidate collapses on real data (and is worst exactly on overdispersed direct-capture, 0.00/0.10). The simple ambient test and fishash are essentially tied (0.950 vs 0.942), and fishash wins the two direct-capture (overdispersed) samples — its simulator overdispersion wobble does not manifest on real overdispersed data.

8 The canonical improvement: decontaminate the cell margin

The marginal-NB failure above was instructive: it failed because a marginal test needs the absolute rate to be exactly right, whereas fishash’s conditional (contingency) test self-calibrates. So the right move is to improve inside the conditional framework. Reading fishash’s source shows a clean, asymmetric gap: fishash’s Simpson correction decontaminates the “other cells” but uses the raw library size N_{:,c} as the focal cell’s exposure (the hypergeometric draws) — it never decontaminates the “other guides in the focal cell.” But our cross-dataset finding is exactly that N_{:,c} is the wrong exposure (library ≠ ambient depth). The canonical, symmetric completion is to decontaminate that entry too, so the cell margin becomes the ambient depth, not the library.

I implemented this as a modular contingency test (scripts/contingency_method.R). With the observed cell margin it reproduces fishash exactly (identical assignments); swapping to the ambient-depth margin is a clean one-factor ablation.

This is a genuine, motivated, performant win — and it targets fishash’s documented weak spot.

  • Simulations: the depth fix beats fishash for MOI ≥ 1 (per-guide F1 0.96 / 0.93 / 0.89 at MOI 1 / 3 / 5 vs fishash 0.96 / 0.89 / 0.82), ties at low MOI, FDR controlled throughout. fishash’s own Fig. 6 shows it loses at MOI ≥ 1 — we now have the mechanism (contaminated cell margin) and the fix.
  • Real barnyard: the depth fix ties fishash (0.937 vs 0.942, no regression), including on the overdispersed direct-capture samples — it doesn’t hurt where the high-MOI advantage doesn’t apply.

The overdispersion tail — an honest negative. I also built the canonical overdispersed conditional tail (NB, the stable Poisson-limit of the beta-binomial; φ estimated from the noise). On the simulator it works — it rescues FDR under overdispersion (0.199 → 0.054 at controlled recall). But on real barnyard it collapses (Table-2 0.02): the φ estimator that I tuned on the simulator produces a wildly wrong dispersion on real data, exactly as the standalone marginal NB did. φ estimation is the genuinely hard, non-robust part — which is why fishash’s plain equidispersed hypergeometric is a wise choice, and it already handles real overdispersed (direct-capture) data well. So: do not deploy the overdispersion tail; keep the hypergeometric. Overdispersion remains open, but low-value (fishash is fine on real overdispersed data).

9 Recommendation

Adopt fishash’s contingency core (Fisher test + Simpson correction + Guo–Sarkar FDR), and apply our one canonical improvement — decontaminate the cell margin (use ambient depth, not library size). This is the “method of our own” that holds up: it is the symmetric completion of fishash’s own decontamination, motivated directly by our cross-dataset depth finding, and it beats fishash at high MOI while tying everywhere else (sims and real data) at controlled FDR. Do not ship the bare ambient test as the flagship, do not pursue the from-scratch marginal NB, and do not deploy an overdispersion tail (φ is not robustly estimable on real data). The evidence:

  1. Accuracy on real, unbiased ground truth: fishash (0.942) \(\approx\) ambient (0.950) on barnyard, and fishash wins the overdispersed direct-capture samples.
  2. Statistical calibration: fishash is the only method that controls per-guide FDR across Simpson and overdispersion at high recall. The simple ambient test is not FDR-calibrated — a real liability for a flagship method supporting genome-scale inference.
  3. Speed/scale: fishash runs in seconds at <1 GiB even at 80,000 guides — like the ambient test, unlike CLEANSER’s MCMC.
  4. It is understood and reproduced: we have independently verified its Simpson correction and FDR behavior; adopting it is not a black box.

On “a method of our own.” The honest scientific finding is that the most natural from-scratch design (decontaminated rank-1 mean + NB tail) is dominated by fishash, for a principled reason — a global overdispersion parameter cannot simultaneously control FDR and preserve power, whereas conditioning sidesteps the problem. So our contribution should be on top of the contingency core, not a replacement of it:

  • A transparent re-derivation + reference implementation of the contingency/Simpson method (we have most of the understanding and reproduction already) — valuable for the SCEPTRE3 ecosystem and not a black-box dependency.
  • Targeted, principled improvements to fishash’s acknowledged soft spots: the conservatism of the GS correction (adaptive \(\pi_0\)), and the rank-1-vs-rank-2 noise mismatch. These are incremental and defensible.
  • The simple ambient test remains a justified fast default for high-signal data and for QC/triage — but labeled as such, not as the rigorous method.

Honest caveats. (i) The simulator is fishash’s own and may favor its test; but the barnyard is real and unbiased and still ranks fishash \(\approx\) ambient \(\gg\) NB. (ii) I tested one novel design family (global-\(\phi\) NB tail). A depth-stratified empirical-null tail is the one untested idea, but these results (plug-in overdispersion is fragile; fishash already handles real overdispersed data) make it low expected value. (iii) All sim metrics are per-guide FDR/recall; the barnyard is per-cell Table-2 — the two agree on the ranking, which is reassuring.
